newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African opposition party mulls government role.
newsitem.headline: S.African opposition party mulls government role.

text.p: South Africa's Democratic Party, which has been in opposition for nearly four decades, said on Wednesday it was studying a suggestion from President Nelson Mandela that it take a role in his government.
Party leader Tony Leon told a news conference the party "adopted a positive approach to President Mandela's suggestion that the DP could play a part in the government of national unity".
The Democratic Party was formed in 1959 as the Progressive Party, whose Helen Suzman was for 13 years the only opponent of apartheid in the whites-only parliament.

The party, whose supporters are mainly relatively affluent whites, gained 1.7 percent of the votes in South Africa's first all-race election in April 1994, giving it seven out of 400 seats in parliament.
It has repeatedly criticised Mandela's government over a range of issues from wasteful spending to lack of accountability.
Leon told the news conference no decision had been made on whether to accept a cabinet post if his party was offered one.
"We will seek the earliest opportunity to discuss with the President Mandela the terms under which we could participate in government without in any compromising our fundamental principles," he said.

The opposition Inkatha Freedom Party of Mangosuthu Buthelezi already serves in the government of national unity and under provisions of the now-defunct interim constitution can continue to do so until the next election in 1999.
The biggest opposition party, F.W. de Klerk's National Party, pulled out of the unity government last year. It said it wanted to take a more active opposition stance.
